In [[probability theory]], a [[stochastic process]] is said to be '''continuous in probability''' or '''stochastically continuous''' if its distributions converge whenever the values in the index set converge. <ref name="applebaum" /><ref name="KallebergFoundations286" />

== Definition ==
Let <math> X=(X_t)_{t \in T} </math> be a [[stochastic process]] in <math> \R^n </math>.
The process <math> X</math> is continuous in probability when <math> X_r </math> [[Convergence in probability|converges in probability]] to <math> X_s </math> whenever <math> r </math> converges to <math> s </math>.<ref name="KallebergFoundations286" />

== Examples and Applications ==
[[Feller process]]es are continuous in probability at <math> t=0 </math>. Continuity in probability is a sometimes used as one of the defining property for [[Lévy process]].<ref name="applebaum" /> Any process that is continuous in probability and has [[independent increments]] has a [[version (probability theory)|version]] that is [[càdlàg]].<ref name="KallebergFoundations286" /> As a result, some authors immediately define Lévy process as being càdlàg and having independent increments.<ref name="KallebergFoundations290" />
